OMG the common formulation of the "bitter lesson" is quite stupid

I mean yes Alpha Zero is "brute force" ish in a way, but is also a genuine algorithmic and architectural innovation -- it's not like any random CS undergrad with a big computer could have trivially coded a standard RL algo to beat Go...

It's like saying a brain just needs a lot of cells to be smart --- well, no ... it probably does need a lot of cells if it uses a standard biological sort of dynamics, but it also needs the right architecture and a lot of other well-honed particulars.   The fact that hand-engineering a brain from a small number of cells works poorly, does not imply that having a large number of cells is the whole secret to biological brains' intelligence...

There is a difference btw a necessary condition and a sufficient condition, folks... (and also a difference btw a necessary condition and a "necessary to make things not extremely laborious" condition...)

It is unfortunate that public dialogue on AI is stuck at this sort of elementary level, but unfortunately the style of discourse of famous AI big-shots does not always help the situation...

fullText:
Brilliant paper on agent memory from FAIR at Meta.

(bookmark it)

A single global history is the usual way to let agents learn from past runs. When tasks are interleaved, it gains almost nothing over no memory at all, an average of +0.015 in normalized reward.

This work proposes Routed Continual Learning. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, and each cluster keeps its state in one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM router reuses a cluster or creates a new one.

They tested it on a stream mixing 301 CL-Bench instances with 97 banking instances from τ³-Bench, across four language models.

Routed CL raised reward over the global history by 15% to 30% of the maximum attainable reward. Estimated API cost fell by 65% to 72%.

The runs were sequential, so parallel agents updating one cluster remain untested.

If your agents handle mixed work, it might help to split their memory into clusters before adding a bigger memory system.

https://t.co/gs8VC9jYCN

fullText:
Banger paper from IBM on decision gates for agents.

They add a runtime gate to tool-using agents and keep the models and tools the same.

JevAct is a check that sits between the agent and its tools. An LLM first turns the domain policy into code checks and yes/no questions. Before a selected tool call runs, the code checks the facts in the tool records, and a Jev-like decision model answers the questions about the conversation. If the call fails a check, it goes back to the agent with feedback so the agent can revise it.

On τ²-bench Telecom, Opus 4.6's success across all three runs rose from 39.5% to 80.7%.

On Telecom, all eight agents improved by 16.9 points on average in three-run success. All nine improved on BFCL. Airline results were smaller and mixed.

They show that the gains come from the harness.

https://t.co/KptDQtLEdO

fullText:
DeepSeek Harness刚刚提出：Super-agent，迈向更自主的Agent系统

来自DeepSeek Harness刚发布的工程架构构想，当单个Coding Agent越来越能独立做事后，如何把Agent从“一个会话一个任务”的工具，变成持续在线、跨会话、能并行推进多任务的数字协作者

直白讲，就是现在很多AI Agent就像按会话分配的临时工，这个Session修Bug，那个Session写代码，另一个Session查看CI，任务一多，人就成了切换器和记事本

所以真正卡生产力的目前不是模型会不会做单个任务，而是人的注意力管不过来这么多并行任务

DeepSeek Harness团队提出了一个Super-agent，就是把这些管理工作交给系统

用户感知层只跟同一个助手说话，一个统一的Super-agent，底层由多个独立的Worker并行执行任务

核心设计包括：
1、Router+Worker双层架构：Router负责全局上下文、任务分派和对外交互，多个Worker在隔离的Session中并行执行任务

2、事件驱动+主动执行：持续接收群聊、GitHub PR、CI 等环境事件，通过规则和模型判断是否需要行动，而不是等待用户逐条下指令

3、异步执行+上下文管理：后台任务运行时仍能接收新指令，通过Inline&Spill、链式召回等机制按需管理上下文，减少不必要的信息注入与工具调用

4、持久运行+Watchdog：将Agent计算、会话状态和执行环境解耦，支持跨设备持续运行，并通过独立Watchdog监控任务进展、检测异常和尝试恢复

研究团队展示了一个内部实践案例：
有人在群聊中反馈 Bug，即使没有@ Agent，Super-agent 也能主动识别问题、尝试复现和修复，并提交GitHub Pull Request

不过，实验使用合成负载和模拟编码任务，验证的主要是多任务调度与协作效率，并不是证明模型写代码的能力提升了

该团队也指出了未解决的问题，包括跨月长程记忆、大规模 Worker协同、权限隔离、提示词注入，以及云端Agent控制本地设备带来的安全风险等

这个架构的部分设计已在dsh-superagent-prototype中实现，这个插件也只是一种为了验证技术路线，并非DeepSeek的正式产品

#Superagent  #DeepSeekHarness #自主式AI

fullText:
Deterministic tests > Written instructions

Anything that should be checked automatically should have a test case:

• Checking behavior → Unit and integration tests
• Checking formatting → Formatters and linters
• Checking types → Static type checkers
• Checking API contracts → Schema validation
• Checking edge cases → Targeted tests
• Checking regressions → Regression tests
• Checking security → Static analysis and security scans

Don't waste tokens telling an agent to follow rules you could enforce with deterministic tests.

Here is my review:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗢𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲

This massive book is incredible, with its comprehensive coverage of numerous fields of mathematics and their intersection with the world of AI, data science, and machine learning (AI+DSML). I remember the very first time that I encountered machine learning. This was 20+ years ago, and that was already after 20+ years of being drenched in advanced mathematics as an astrophysicist. 

That first encounter of mine with ML was this definition: "Machine learning is the set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience" (slightly paraphrased from the original quote by Tom Mitchell, CMU). That definition surprised me, confused me, motivated me, and changed the course of my career from astrophysics into AI+DSML. 

This book by Tivadar Danka captures the full meaning of that definition. The book covers thoroughly the many areas and domains of mathematics through which patterns in data are detected, described, learned, and recognized - all for the benefit of powering ML and AI algorithms, applications, and aspirations. 

This book will motivate you, surprise you, and inspire you in many ways, no matter what level of mathematics has (or has not) already propelled your career journey. There is room for all of us to grow. 

This is a great book, worthy to sit on everyone's desktop, ready to help you explore and exploit the full set of mathematical algorithms that learn from experience. 

The book is accompanied by a rich GitHub code repository of Jupyter notebooks. Learn by doing! Do by learning!

Disclosure: the publisher provided me with a free review copy of the book.

fullText:
Inspired by the spinor nature of spin–orbit-coupled electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features to predict spin-orbit coupling (SOC)-dependent magnetic properties.

Magnetic properties such as magnetic anisotropy, excitation energies, and spin dynamics guide the design of single-molecule magnets, MRI probes, and other spin-based technologies. Predicting them often requires CASSCF-SO calculations to capture multireference electronic structure, which can take hours for a single molecular geometry.

SO(3)-equivariance has improved the accuracy of rotation-invariant energy predictions in machine-learning interatomic potentials. Can we take this idea further by imposing SU(2)-equivariance on spinor features as an inductive bias for predicting magnetic properties?

Our main contributions are:
(1) SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing: Hamiltonian-derived spinors and classified interaction types enable gauge-covariant updates and gauge-invariant predictions
(2) Unseen-ligand generalization: Improved magnetic anisotropy and excitation-energy predictions for cobalt and dysprosium single-molecule magnet candidates
(3) Spin dynamics and solvent transfer: More accurate predictions for a dysprosium MRI probe, with benefits extending from water to methanol without retraining

Our results support SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism, even when the targets are integer-rank tensors or invariant scalars.

With this framework, we’re excited to help accelerate the discovery of new magnetic molecules and deepen our understanding of their spin dynamics!

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.
